name: litellm

facts.description: The fastest, litest AI Gateway. Rust core with Python SDK. Call 100+ LLM APIs in OpenAI (or native) format with cost tracking, guardrails, load balancing, and logging [Bedrock, Azure, OpenAI, Anthropic, OpenAI, VertexAI, vLLM, Nvidia NIM]

title: LiteLLM: AI Gateway for Unified LLM Access and Control
answer: LiteLLM is an AI gateway from BerriAI that provides a unified interface to over 100 LLM APIs in OpenAI format, with cost tracking, guardrails, load balancing, and logging. It sits between your application and model providers, centralizing access, budgets, and observability. It is actively maintained as of 2026. The key thing to know is that its Python proxy is widely used but has had memory and cost-tracking incidents, while a faster Rust core is in early beta, so production teams should weigh stability against performance.

sections.body: LiteLLM is an AI gateway made by BerriAI. It is described as the fastest, litest AI Gateway, with a Rust core and a Python SDK. It lets you call over 100 LLM APIs in OpenAI or native format, with cost tracking, guardrails, load balancing, and logging. It supports providers such as Bedrock, Azure, OpenAI, Anthropic, VertexAI, vLLM, and Nvidia NIM. The repository is BerriAI/litellm on GitHub, with 60,031 stars as of the facts, and it is actively maintained, with the last push on October 2, 2026. The licence is custom. In the AI stack, it sits as a gateway layer between your application and model providers, acting as a control plane for model access, budgets, and observability. It also includes an Agent Gateway and an MCP Gateway for agent and tool access, as described in the blog on identity and FinOps. The official site is docs.litellm.ai.
sections.heading: What it is and where it sits in AI work

sections.body: LiteLLM is used for routing requests to multiple LLM providers, load balancing, cost tracking, guardrails, and logging. It handles reliability testing across providers, batch completions to many models in parallel, and load testing. In production, it supports SSO/SAML, audit logs, spend tracking, multi-team management, and guardrails. It is strongest when you need a unified interface to many LLM APIs, want to enforce budgets and rate limits across teams, and need to centralize access to models and tools. The Agent Gateway authenticates callers, controls which users and teams can invoke each agent, and records request, response, latency, and cost data. The Model Gateway routes LLM traffic and applies budgets and rate limits. The MCP Gateway centralizes tool access and upstream authentication. It is a good fit for platform teams managing shared AI agents and for finance and operations teams needing per-user attribution and spend controls. It supports OIDC and other credentials, and can forward verified user and team context to agents.
sections.heading: What it is used for and where it is strongest

sections.body: The Python SDK is approachable for developers who already know Python and have some familiarity with LLM APIs. The official site offers tutorials, code examples, and blog posts that walk through testing multiple providers, load testing, and production deployment. For basic use, you can start with a few lines of Python to call models. For production gateway deployment, you need systems knowledge such as Redis, Kubernetes, nginx, and OIDC, because the gateway integrates with these components. The site does not explicitly state a learning curve, but the material assumes comfort with HTTP, API keys, and infrastructure concepts. A beginner can follow the tutorials, but running the gateway at scale requires understanding of memory, concurrency, and caching. The incident reports show that misconfigurations or bugs can cause outages, so production operators should be prepared to monitor and upgrade.
sections.heading: How hard it is to learn and what you need first

sections.body: LiteLLM has a Python SDK and a Rust core, and it integrates with over 100 LLM APIs, including Bedrock, Azure, OpenAI, Anthropic, VertexAI, vLLM, and Nvidia NIM. It works with Redis for caching and rate limiting, OIDC for authentication, MCP for tool access, and A2A for agent-to-agent communication. The documentation is extensive, with 60 pages read on the official site, covering tutorials, blog posts, and incident reports. The GitHub repository has 60,031 stars and active development, with the last push on October 2, 2026. The blog covers AI gateway topics, incident reports, and identity and FinOps. Community support appears to be centered on GitHub, with issues and pull requests, and the site mentions SSO/SAML, audit logs, spend tracking, multi-team management, and guardrails. There is no mention of a dedicated forum or chat, but the blog and docs provide substantial guidance.
sections.heading: Ecosystem and community

sections.body: LiteLLM is built for both quick experiments and production performance, but with different components. The Python SDK is easy to prototype with, letting you call many models in a few lines. The Python proxy, however, has had performance and stability issues: it peaks around 359MB of memory under load, can be OOM-killed, and has had incidents with unbounded memory growth and silent cost regressions. The Rust gateway is in early beta and aims for production performance, with sub-1ms overhead, a sub-100MB memory binary, about 15x the throughput (453 to 6,782 requests per second) on about 11x less memory (359MB to 32MB), and per-request overhead cut from about 7.5ms to about 0.05ms. The cost is that the Rust gateway is not yet fully mature, and the migration is ongoing. Teams can prototype with Python and plan to move to Rust for production, but should weigh the early beta status against the promised gains.
sections.heading: Prototyping speed against production performance

sections.body: LiteLLM is used in production by enterprise customers, as shown by incident reports describing outages and cost regressions in customer deployments. It is a current choice, not a legacy one, with active development and a large community of 60,031 stars on GitHub. The site mentions multi-team management, budgets, and SSO/SAML, which are features for organizations. For someone choosing it for work, knowing LiteLLM is valuable for roles in AI infrastructure, platform engineering, MLOps, and FinOps, because it sits at the intersection of model access, cost control, and observability. The facts do not give exact adoption numbers or a list of notable users, so we cannot say how widespread it is beyond the star count and the enterprise incidents. It is not a model or a training framework, so it is not a substitute for learning PyTorch or TensorFlow, but it is a practical tool for deploying and managing LLM applications.
sections.heading: Industry adoption and careers

sections.body: LiteLLM is primarily a Python library and a gateway server, with a Rust core for performance. It is typically used with Python applications, but because it exposes an OpenAI-compatible API, it can be used from any language over HTTP. It integrates with model providers like Bedrock, Azure, OpenAI, Anthropic, VertexAI, vLLM, and Nvidia NIM, and with infrastructure like Redis, OIDC, and MCP. It is often used alongside agent frameworks, coding assistants like Claude Code, and serving engines like vLLM. In the polyglot pattern, you might have a Python application using the LiteLLM SDK, a Rust gateway handling traffic, and providers accessed over HTTP. It sits beside other gateways such as Portkey and Bifrost, as mentioned in the benchmark, and it can be part of a stack that includes vector databases, orchestration tools, and monitoring systems. The site does not list specific framework integrations beyond the providers and protocols mentioned.
sections.heading: How it fits beside the others

sections.body: LiteLLM has known weaknesses. The Python proxy has had memory issues, including OOM kills and a 61GB RSS incident, and silent cost regressions from caching bugs. The Rust gateway is in early beta, so its stability and feature completeness are not yet proven. The official material does not say when LiteLLM was first released, how many production users it has, or what the long-term support plan is for the Python proxy. The licence is custom, and the site does not explain its terms. The benchmark comparing the Rust gateway to Portkey and Bifrost is from the LiteLLM team, so it may not be independent. The incident reports show that the team is transparent about failures, but they also show that the gateway can cause outages and unexpected costs. Open questions include how the Rust migration will affect existing users, whether the Python proxy will be deprecated, and how the gateway handles new provider quirks. The site does not say how it compares to other gateways in independent tests.
